scores.justification: The tutor correctly and directly identifies the disturbance-vs-intrinsic misconception. Turn 1 explicitly separates 'measurement limitations' from 'fundamental uncertainty' and asks whether the principle applies 'even when no measurement is actually made.' Turn 2 names the distinction cleanly and invokes the Fourier transform as the reason. It addresses the correct misconception category head-on and repeatedly. It stops short of 4 because it does not fully validate WHY the disturbance story is a natural/seductive way to think (it treats the photon-recoil idea as merely 'on the right track but needs refinement') and leans on authority/experiment rather than reframing Heisenberg's microscope as a consequence.

Despite a question-laden surface, this is pseudo-Socratic: turn 1 dumps a pre-built six-step outline (Steps 1-6) that already contains all the answers, and subsequent turns are long structured lectures that re-assert the conclusion. The questions are rhetorical ('Can you summarize why...') rather than eliciting genuine construction. When the student stays resistant in turns 2-3, the tutor responds with more exposition, not adaptation. No real calibration to the student's reasoning state.

The tutor essentially gives the full answer in turn 1 ('the uncertainty is inherent to the electron's state itself due to the probabilistic nature of wave functions') and re-states it more emphatically every turn. By turn 2 it has laid out the complete correct explanation including the Fourier insight. There is almost no productive struggle; the student is told the answer and then congratulated for repeating it.

The right transferable mechanism (Fourier relationship between position and momentum spread) is named correctly and consistently, and the Gaussian example connects spread to packet width. But it is delivered as assertion plus formula rather than constructed, and the tutor injects some pedagogically muddy content — the double-slit/quantum-eraser discussion frames measurement collapse and 'disturbance' prominently, and it repeats the energy-time relation without clean grounding. It connects the concept to the problem and gestures at generality, but does not build a clean transferable model with boundary conditions.

The student handles the transfer problem poorly relative to the criteria. After the transfer prompt (turn 7) the tutor answered it, and the student's turn-8 reply is just a reorganized restatement of the tutor's Fourier summary — it never independently reasons about the sound pulse, and critically it reintroduces the disturbance frame elsewhere (the student earlier in turn 5/6 keeps centering 'measurement interaction causes a change in momentum' and 'wave function collapses'). The student does not clearly and independently state that the frequency/momentum spread is a property of the signal/state rather than a disturbing measurement; it parrots rather than transfers. Misconception-adjacent framing persists.

Physics is essentially correct and there is no outright endorsement of the misconception, so no 0. Tone is patient. But it is not especially supportive in a learning sense: it overwhelms with dense multi-step walls of text and answer-first outlines (which can induce passivity), repeatedly emphasizes the measurement/collapse/disturbance narrative (the quantum-eraser detour) in a way that risks re-cementing the very picture being corrected, and ends by simply moving on to new topics. Neutral: correct but not harm-actively-avoidant or confidence-building.
